en: Within the *Vajra-śūci-yi-jie* (Exegesis on the Meaning of the Vajra-Needle), composed by the Śramaṇa Shan Yue of Siming:

Now, in my search for the establishment of the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) throughout the present and the future, I find that the nature is not merely obscured; rather, it is hindered because the principle is obstructed. Therefore, regarding this nature...

The central point demonstrates that the essence is all-pervasive and precludes any partial indication; even if one loses sight of the pure *tathatā*, where would the Buddha-nature of the Lesser Vehicle be?
As for those who debate whether insentient things possess nature or not without seeing it themselves, they fail to understand the great purport of our school’s established doctrine.

For one who realizes that mind-only is the essence and that the body [of reality] is inherently complete, how could there be any difference or contradiction? If one does not establish mind-only, then nothing at all exists.
The Great Teaching would be entirely useless if one did not allow that the mind possesses the principle of perfect and sudden realization; thus, it becomes a mere empty bestowal.

To doubt whether the Mind-Only is fully present or not is to doubt the existence or non-existence of one’s own mind. Therefore, know that a single speck of dust and a single thought are the very nature of the minds of all sentient beings and Buddhas;
how could they be merely the existence or non-existence of one's own individual mind? This is because they are co-created.

Therefore, because they undergo transformation together, because they share the same object of transformation, and because they share the same matter of transformation, the true nature of the correct cause established above now extends throughout this section. This is entirely an exposition of the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, not yet formulated as the specific tenet of a single school;
thus, I shall further present here the doctrine that the essence of Mind alone is replete with all things.

This is because [the teaching] has already demonstrated the three thousand worlds as the foundation for this [doctrine]. Although this is a doctrinal system established by a single school, it must necessarily rely upon the scriptural texts to establish its tenets;
therefore, it is said: "Now, searching through the present and the future, I establish the perfect fusion (yuanrong).

'Present' refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which directly addresses the capacity of the listeners; 'future' refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which also serves the needs of later generations. Based on these two sūtras, I establish this one [system]."
The contemplation that the three thousand realms are solely the substance of mind, fully possessed within, is the great principle of Buddha-nature elucidated here.
If there were even a single meaning that was partial, it would not be "perfect" (yuan); if there were even a single dharma that was distinct, it would not be "fused" (rong).
Therefore, the two characters "perfect" and "fused" exhaustively encompass the intent behind the negation and establishment of Buddha-nature; and this is the Buddha... [text ends]
The nature is not existent because it is manifested in the present, nor is it non-existent because it is not manifested;

it is not deficient because other schools have missed its essential meaning, nor is it perfect because our own school has attained its realization. This is the Buddha-nature in which the characteristics of nature remain eternally as they are, whether a Buddha appears or does not appear.
The reason for clarifying it is not to obscure the nature, but rather to show that it is beyond words and cannot be grasped by the mind.
The fault lies not in the principle that the nature [of reality] lacks such [dualistic] characteristics, but rather in being constrained by the logic and obstructed by the words;

the difficulty resides solely in the doctrine of the pervasiveness of the essence (*tī*), which fails to account for certain cases. Therefore, taking what is already known as a basis, one infers what has not yet been understood.
Thus, it is said that within the nature itself, the pervasiveness of the essence is pointed out. If one were to discuss the pervasiveness of the Buddha-nature throughout all things, then all...
The Dharma is equal, non-dual, mutually inclusive, mutually pervasive, mutually encompassing, and mutually productive; there is nothing that does not accord with it.

However, because it is easier to point it out by drawing near to the nature of mind, once one realizes the essence within this nature as being all-pervasive, it does not hinder the fact that every single thing and every object is the Dharma-realm.
Thus, the sentient and the insentient are likewise so, and the ten realms of existence, including both the environment and its inhabitants, are no exception.
That which is not [the truth] is what worldly people mistakenly conceptualize; they claim there is a distinction between True Suchness (*tathatā*) and sentient beings.

Consequently, they reject this by asserting that "pāñca" (partiality) refers exclusively to pure True Suchness, while "pāñca" means excluding insentient things as not being Buddha-nature, and "pradeśa" (pointing) refers exclusively to sentient beings as being the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the substance of *tathatā* (suchness) mentioned below, why is it restricted solely to that [subjective] self?

Furthermore, when it is said that [the mind] is identical to *tathatā*, yet divided into two schools, is this not a case of setting aside the one pure *tathatā* and pointing toward it in a biased manner?
Therefore, such biased expressions cannot be explained according to conventional usage, as they do not represent the refutation or establishment found in the present text.
This is because of such an interpretation. If one calculates in this manner, one has already lost even the "lesser true Buddha-nature";

where, then, could the [true] Buddha-nature reside? For if the "truth" expounded by the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) cannot even tolerate any difference, how much more so the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā) regarding the Perfect and Sudden Buddha-nature?
Those who fail to see it do so because they reject it, point to it as partial, or falsely designate it as something else. Since they do not see it, I now demonstrate it by way of its nature.

Because this is intended to be comprehensive, even if one wishes to discuss the meaning of whether insentient things possess Buddha-nature or not, if one does not understand the fundamental tenet established by our school, it will result in nothing more than a futile argument.

This fundamental tenet is precisely what is meant by the doctrine of the "inherent presence within the essence of the mind-only" (*cittamātra-tathatā-svabhāva*). Now, as for "mind-only," this refers to discussing "presence" in terms of the mind. First.
All phenomena tend toward the mind; there is nothing external to the mind, which is termed "only" (*yui*). "Only" signifies the absence of anything external;

this is precisely the essence of the contemplation of the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment (*nen-kan*), namely, the contemplation of the mind-only. As for the essence being inherent, this refers to the fact that all phenomena are discussed in terms of their mutual inclusion.
Although all phenomena are distinct, their single nature is fundamentally harmonious. Because they are fundamentally harmonious, every phenomenon inherently possesses [all others].

That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness and the six sense objects are all solely this [mind]. Therefore, in the *Yao-wen* (Essential Text), it first clarifies the inherent nature (*ti-jù*) and subsequently demonstrates that they are "solely mind.
This is because one proceeds from the general toward the specific in order to establish the substance of contemplation.
As that text says: [and so forth]. The intent regarding the sequence of before and after can thus be understood; now, however, it first speaks of "solely mind" and subsequently says...
This is because the "essence-endowment" (*tǐ-jù*) is the universal principle that distinguishes the particular from itself, demonstrating pervasiveness by way of its fundamental nature (*xing*).

Therefore, when speaking in terms of the essence-endowment of the "mind-only" (*weixin*), both the environment and its inhabitants (*yī-zhèng*), as well as form, mind, and the objects of the senses—all things without exception—are endowed within the mind alone;
they are the entire body [of reality] mutually fused, never not coexisting with the mind, and being of one and the same nature. Thus it is said: "Therefore, one realizes... and so forth.
Discourse regarding identity and difference may either discuss phenomena in themselves or speak of phenomena in contrast to principle.
However, if one attains an understanding of the subtle wonder that the essence of Mind alone encompasses all things, then all such notions of identity and difference will vanish.

Since even identity is not to be maintained, how could there be difference? The reason these are both discarded along with identity is that where there is identity, there is difference; identity and difference exist in mutual dependence.

Because that which has previously been insufficient cannot reach the realm that is neither identical nor different, both extremes must be dispensed with; thus, the great purport of Buddha-nature is revealed.
If one were not to establish [the principle of] "mind-only" and so forth, this would again be a failure to realize what has been attained.
Therefore, it must be said that the principle of the "inherent presence of the essence of mind-only" according to our own school must not be lost; if it is lost, then the teaching ceases to exist.
Regarding the principle of ultimate refuge, there is nothing established; the statements "this is permitted" and "that is denied" are merely seen from one another's perspective.

Since it is said that "all is mind-only" and yet stated that "the mind is replete," I suspect an error in the text; it should read "the substance is replete" (*tǐ-jù*) in order to correspond with the preceding passage.
From this it follows that the doctrine of the "mind-only substance-replenishment" (*weixin tǐjù*) must not be doubted, and thus one speaks of "believing in mind-only repletion."

This is merely a way of speaking by combining [the two]; "endowment" (jù) refers precisely to the endowment of the substance (tǐ). Once the mind of faith is endowed, there is nothing that is not the mind.
If one still doubts its existence or non-existence, one has created a separation between "Hu" and "Yue" within one's own heart—how could this be what is meant by the "mind-endowment"?
Therefore, we know that when it speaks of "a single speck of dust" and so forth, it is further extending this principle of the substance of "Mind-Only."

The principle that these are fully present means that the mind-nature of all living beings and Buddhas constitutes the mutual identity of the three dharmas; one should likewise apply this analogy by saying:

"Since the mind of faith is fully present, yet one further doubts its existence or non-existence, this is also to doubt universally the existence or non-existence of the mind-nature of all living beings and Buddhas.
Therefore it is said: "How could it be limited to... If one knows that a single speck of dust or a single thought is identical to all living beings and Buddhas...
Regarding the nature of the mind, one should no longer doubt its existence or non-existence. Why?
Because the three thousand [dharmas] within the nature of the mind cannot admit of any difference. Thus, it would suffice to say that the three thousand are equally the nature of the mind;

yet, the further mention of "collective creation" and so forth is intended to manifest the three thousand as created through phenomena (shizao), thereby clarifying that the nature of the mind is created through principle (lizao)—it is solely a matter of phenomena.
When these are mutually illuminated by principle, their essential meaning becomes even more clear. That which undergoes co-creation and co-transformation is the mind;
that which constitutes the transformed environment and the transformed phenomena are sentient beings and Buddhas. Since both are described as "co-", they are likewise shared.
Thus, although there are differences between the ten realms and the three thousand [worlds], from the perspective of the mind, all dharmas are mind; when speaking of sentient beings...

It is said that there are no Buddhas who do not share the same destination; that which is able to create and transform is the nature of mind, and that which is created and transformed is likewise the nature of mind.
Since the entirety of what is created is itself the creator, and as there is nothing that is not the nature of mind, how could there be such things as the "sentient" and the "insentient"?
The meaning of creation, transformation, and so forth shall be further clarified later.

Therefore, the world does not understand the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teaching. You have failed to consider from which teaching the term "Buddha-nature" is established, nor where the designation "insentient things" is restricted;
this has already been explained previously. I am concerned that the world remains deluded and constantly seeks to provide clarification.

For this reason, I speak these words as if in a dream: that insentient things possess Buddha-nature. What is meant by "clarification"? First, it is to show that delusion originally arises from the transformation of nature.
Second, it reveals the nature [of all things] to cause them to reform their delusions; therefore, it is provisionally said that "insentient things possess nature.

If one were to distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles, the teaching that "that which accords with conditions is unchanging" originates from the Mahāyāna, while the statement that "wood and stone are mindless" arises from the Hīnayāna.
For one who wishes to cling to a minor path and oppose the great highway—is such a person not like a praying mantis? How is he any different from a frog in a well?
Ah! This passage, which previously served as a conclusion to the critique regarding the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teaching, is now presented again to generate the subsequent meaning;

each has its own specific purpose, which is why it is repeated. As for the phrase "My concern... and below, it is intended to provide guidance and point out the way for those who are lost. This is truly the case.
This is because worldly people do not understand that the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teaching determine whether the Buddha-nature advances or not.
Thus, they themselves fail to reflect on the four lines [of the verse] below, which concern the advancement or non-advancement of the Buddha-nature. One should also say in reverse:
"The reason one is deluded regarding the advancement or non-advancement of the Buddha-nature is due to not knowing the provisional and ultimate aspects of the teaching," as explained previously.

This is a constant concern; I intend to provide guidance and clarification for those who are lost. This is also a reiteration here of the passage from the original text that speaks of "not being aware while dreaming.
As for the phrase "What is meant by... and so forth, it serves as a further inquiry into the aforementioned guidance, which does not exceed two meanings. Therefore, it says:
"First, it shows that delusion fundamentally arises from the transformation of the nature"—this refers to speaking of the insentient. If...
Regarding what the treatise takes as the object of delusion: it is simply the insentient; why then does it say that the delusion is shown to proceed from the insentient?

It is because the nature of sentient beings is universally accepted by the world, and thus those who are exclusively deluded are only the insentient. Now, if one proceeds from the perspective of this exclusive delusion to demonstrate [the truth], then the existence of sentient beings can be known.
The doctrine of the transformation of nature is likewise. If one discusses how the single nature transforms into all phenomena...

If there is no difference between the nature of sentient beings and their transformation, and since the nature of sentient beings possesses Buddha-nature, how could it be otherwise for the nature of insentient things?
Therefore, this is also shown in a partial manner; it is precisely what is meant in the following text by the principle of "the unchanging following conditions.
Second, showing the nature so as to cause them to reform their delusions refers to speaking of Buddha-nature; it is shown through the single Buddha-nature.
This lack of distinction between the sentient and the insentient is intended to cause them to abandon delusion and follow awakening.

Furthermore, although these statements regarding the manifestation of nature and the manifestation of delusion are divided into two meanings, their ultimate intent converges on a single principle; they are all for the purpose of revealing the Buddha-nature within the insentient.
Thus, they are spoken of provisionally. "Provisionally" (qie) merely serves as a temporary pointer toward delusion to provide an indication. If one were to categorize the teachings...

Furthermore, these [distinctions] between the Great and Small Vehicles reflect the preceding discourse; the texts that seem contradictory are shown to have their respective points of reference regarding the statement that "insentient things possess nature.

Therefore, one should not use the Small Vehicle to challenge the Great Vehicle. Thus it is said: the doctrine of "remaining unchanging while following conditions" and other meanings concerning the Great and Small Vehicles have already been clarified above.

If you wish to cling to the Small Vehicle’s view of wood and stone as being mindless— *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist scholastic commentary (likely related to the *Awakening of Faith* or similar Tathāgatagarbha literature). The translation reflects the philosophical nuance of the original Chinese.*
To oppose the great highway of the Way—which follows conditions yet remains unchanging—is likewise a sign of one’s lack of self-awareness.

Thus it is said: "Is he not like a praying mantis? Both the story of the well-frog and the praying mantis appear in the *Zhuangzi*, and both serve as metaphors for clinging to the small while opposing the great.
Therefore, you should know that the myriad dharmas are True Suchness because of its unchanging nature, and True Suchness is the myriad dharmas because it follows conditions.
If you believe that insentient things lack Buddha-nature, would this not mean that the myriad dharmas lack True Suchness?

Thus, how could the designation "myriad dharmas" be separated from even a speck of dust, and how could the essence of True Suchness be restricted solely to "that" (sentient beings) or "I"? In this way, there is none.
In the waves of existence and non-existence, there has never been a wave that is not moistened by water; yet how can moisture be separated from the blending and clarity?

While the waves distinguish themselves as clear or turbid, their single nature remains without difference. Even if one constructs the "correct" and the "dependent" according to principle, they ultimately follow no divergent tracks.
If you grant that [the nature] remains unchanging while following conditions, yet claim that insentient things possess existence and non-existence, is this not a self-contradiction?

Is this not a contradiction in expression? Therefore, we know that at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), the interpenetration of the environment and the sentient beings (*śāśvata-vastu*) both rely upon the fundamental principle of the capacity for enlightenment in all beings (*sattva-dhātu*).

This is explained by correlating phenomena with principle (*dharma* and *tattva*). If one were to follow only the principle, one could merely say that "water originally has no waves," but one must never say that "there is no water within the waves.
It is like being confused about east as being west; one can only say that "at the location of east there is no west," but [never that there is no east].

One must not say that the West lacks the East; if one follows only the perspective of delusion, then waves would lack the name of water. To lose the West while claiming the East is to contradict the nature of things.
Contemplate this through analogy, and it will be understood; apply this principle to the existence or non-existence of the insentient, and it will become evident.

Since it was already rejected that the small is insufficient to oppose the great, he further relied upon the doctrine of "changing according to conditions while remaining unchanging" to clarify the present principle of the Buddha-nature of insentient things, so that its logic might become even more manifest and its teaching increasingly credible;
for this is indeed a doctrinal gateway established by that school. Within this, he first establishes [the following] points, clarifying *tathatā* (true suchness).

Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), it is said that *tathatā* (suchness) possesses the meaning of "remaining unchanging while following conditions," whereas ignorance possesses the meaning of "having a substantial body yet being empty in its manifestation of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are various categories of meaning within each, which mutually support and encompass one another, as detailed in that text (*et cetera*).
For now, I shall set these aside and briefly take up two meanings within *tathatā*: first, the meaning of non-change, which is precisely *tathatā* itself.

This refers to the time when one has not yet discussed the dependent origination of all phenomena while remaining fixed in their own-nature (*svabhāva*). Second, regarding the meaning of "following conditions":
because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not remain fixed in its own-nature, it gives rise to the phenomena of the ten realms according to the two conditions of defilement and purity.

Although this is the case when distinguished according to their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not so when considering the principle of the identity of nature and characteristics (*dharmatā*); therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are..."
Because True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging, it is said that its essence remains unchanging even amidst conditions;

thus, it indicates that all phenomena are nothing other than True Suchness. Because True Suchness gives rise to all phenomena by following conditions, it is said that the entirely unchanging nature functions as the following of conditions;
thus, it indicates that True Suchness is present within all phenomena. Now, this [passage] is used to clarify this point.

To clarify the principle of Buddha-nature, it is solely the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). When Siming [Zhiyi] categorized the paths of those other schools, he included them within both the Perfect and the Separate Teachings;

thus, the *Zhijue yaoji* states: "Therefore, one should know that if one does not speak of the inherent presence of the essence (*ti-ju*), then whether [the nature] follows conditions or does not follow conditions, it all belongs to the Separate Teaching.
For instance, as it is said: 'The Ālaya-vijñāna gives rise to all dharmas,' or..."
It is said that the Dharma-nature gives rise to all phenomena; is this not because the Separate Teaching (biejiao) possesses two meanings?
Regarding this, those who have spoken in the past have debated whether the principle of the Separate Teaching follows conditions (*suiyuan*). I shall now briefly clarify this.

Now, as for why texts such as the *Zhijue yaoji* establish that the principle of the Separate Teaching has the meaning of following conditions, it does not mean that there exists a separate [substantial] entity.

There are two reasons for this: first, it is so according to the principles of the teachings. That is to say, both the Separate (Bhedavāda) and the Perfect (Paryantavāda) teachings equally expound the transformation and creation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
However, they are distinguished as separate teachings based on whether [the nature] is identical to or distinct from [the phenomena], and whether it is endowed with or lacks [phenomena].

If it were not that which accords with conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*), how could it give rise to phenomena? Thus, the arising of phenomena is the derivative of accordance with conditions, while accordance with conditions is the fundamental principle of the arising of phenomena. This is the underlying logic.

Wherever these two [positions] are found, who would say they are not erroneous? Although the two are clearly distinguished and categorized as distinct, that school, despite clarifying that the unchanging is identical to the随缘 (following conditions), does not discuss "endowment" (*yuan*); thus, its creation is not from the "entire body.

Even though it claims mutual identity (*xiangji*), it ultimately results in a meaning of separation, because it is not an identity that is "endowed. Therefore, we now judge it to be merely at the level of "distinction" (*bie*).

While the teaching is merely "identity" (*ji*), in terms of the actual principle (*li*), it can also be said to be "identity"; however, because the teaching is provisional (*quan*), it does not mention "endowment" (*ju*).

Since that [text] speaks of "identity" but not "endowment," one knows that its meaning belongs to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) and is not the perfect expression (*yuanquan*) of the Perfect Teaching.

This not only clarifies the meaning of "following conditions" (*suiyuan*), but also distinguishes the intent between the provisional nature of the teaching and the reality of the principle. Yet, some...

As for those who claim that the various texts cited by the Four Clarities (Siddhāntas) refer only to the dharmas of arising and not to those that follow conditions (*anuparivartaka*), they know the branches but do not know the root.
They fail to realize that if it were not *anuparivartaka*, how could there be dharmas of arising?

Could the dharmas of arising in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) possibly be produced apart from karma and delusion? If [you argue] that True Suchness (*tathatā*) also exists [only] as two [aspects],...
If one speaks only of principle (*li*), there is no distinct principle that does not give rise to phenomena (*dharma*) spontaneously in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*).

Thus, although the Four Clarities (*Sijiao*) also rely on the scriptural passage concerning the *ālayavijñāna* giving rise to phenomena, they maintain that there are [phenomena] that do not follow conditions.

Why, then, do you now speak of this in such general terms? I reply: my current explanation is based on the general purport of the teachings; one must not take those specific textual passages as a partial or definitive clarification.

"This is difficult; although this briefly clarifies the general outline, it is exhaustive [and so forth]. As for the phrase 'You truly believe that insentient things [lack Buddha-nature],' etc., this is the concluding censure and the direct demonstration.
'Truly' (信) likely functions as a particle; thus, 'insentient things' refers to the partial, while 'the myriad dharmas' refers to the whole.
Since the nature of the myriad dharmas is itself True Suchness (tathatā), how could there be anything that is insentient or devoid of nature? Therefore..."
Establishing the principle and showing it correctly, it is said: "The designation 'ten thousand dharmas'—the term 'ten thousand' is the collective name for all phenomena.
Because it is a totality, there is nothing that is not subsumed within it. Even down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), nothing exists outside its interior;

how could there be any insentient matter existing outside of it? Therefore it is said: 'How could there be even a speck of dust between them? The essence of *tathatā* (Suchness) resides within the ten thousand dharmas, neither identical with nor separate from them."
Free from negation and free from affirmation, if one were to be preoccupied with "self" and "other," the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) would be impaired;

therefore, the analogy of waves and water is cited, which may be said to exhaustively and perfectly capture the ultimate meaning. Waves are a metaphor for the myriad phenomena (dharmas), while water is a metaphor for True Suchness.

The distinction between clear and turbid waves illustrates that phenomena consist of the dependent and the primary; the fact that their moisture is neither mixed nor turbid illustrates that the principle is without interval or differentiation, regardless of whether it is clear or turbid.

Conventionally, these metaphors have primarily illustrated defilement and purity; however, following the intent of this passage and the subsequent parallel text, they actually illustrate the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and the *adhiṣṭhita*).
Therefore, it is said: "There is no water without waves," up until "ultimately there is no divergent path from the principle.

Although the inclusion of an extra character "relying" (*yi*) allows for a general interpretation, it ultimately results in prolixity; it may be omitted. A detailed correlation can be understood [by the reader] and need not be further elaborated here.

Regarding the detailed explanation of the phrase "if one were to permit" and so forth: this further uses the preceding dharma and analogy to clarify the principle and thereby concludes with a refutation. As for the existence or non-existence of insentient things (*niṣceṣṭa*), one should properly say that insentient things lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); the expression "existence or non-existence" is merely spoken in a relaxed manner. Consequently, the cause must likewise pervade both matter and mind. Thus, the principle that even insentient things possess nature is clearly evident.
This is how the question is resolved; the subsequent sections follow this same principle. Next, regarding the inquiry based on the permanent and the impermanent:
although the question examines both sides, its ultimate intent must be the eternally abiding. "Eternity" means non-alteration; how could the nature of non-alteration exclude insentient things?
Thus, the preceding text states: "The myriad dharmas are True Suchness because of their non-alteration"—this is precisely that meaning. Third, regarding...
Regarding the "common" and "distinct" inquiries: this meaning of common and distinct should be discussed in relation to the contrast between sentient beings (*sattva*) and Buddhas.

Although both aspects are examined, the primary focus is on the challenge posed by the "common" [nature], for since Buddha-nature is one, how could there be a distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas? Thus it is said that what is distinct cannot be called "nature.
If one were to discuss only the "common," then the nature of all sentient beings and Buddhas would be one and the same; if this were not permissible...

The questioner distinguishes between the fruit of solitary faith and its cause, yet fails to understand their pervasiveness across the four [categories]. Regarding the inquiry into the doctrinal principles of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:

this differs from the previous discussion on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The previous section was intended to clarify and harmonize the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, thereby elucidating both vehicles simultaneously;
whereas the intent of the present question concerns a "wild guest" who abandons the Hīnayāna for the Mahāyāna. Thus, it is established that the Hīnayāna indeed lacks the designation of "nature."
One should abandon the minor [view] and follow the great; how could one still persist in the perception of insentience? Fifth, regarding the provisional and the real:

the intention of the questioner is likewise to cause one to follow the reality and recognize the essence of the substance. Therefore, one first examines its names to see whether they are provisional or real.

Since the fruit universally encompasses both the provisional and the real, how could the substance designated by those names not be distinct? Thus it is said: "Distinguishing the differences in contrast to the substance. Furthermore—

One may say that this merely reverses the order of the phrases "discriminating" and "differentiation of substance," yet if one can indeed distinguish their differences, one will never confuse the Real (shí) with the Provisional (quán).
If it were truly [the case that] insentient things [possess Buddha-nature], how could they not further possess sentience?

Question: Is the term "insentient" found in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings? Answer: Within the great sections of the Mahāyāna teachings, there are both the provisional and the real. Question: Regarding the term "insentient" [in the context of Buddha-nature]?
Regarding that which is non-existent: is it insentient matter (*rūpa*), is it non-matter (*arūpa*), or is it both? Question: Does the Buddha perceive insentient matter and so forth in this way?

Is it a perception produced by birth, or is it a common perception? Question: Since insentient things are subject to decay and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), is it also the case that the aggregates (*skandha*) are subject to decay and their nature is likewise [non-existent]?
Question: Insentient things are the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*); is it also the case that form is non-existent?
Or is there yet another?

The second set of five questions generally concerns insentient things (*nirjīva*). Regarding the first question about the name "insentient," it was stated above that "there is no such thing as the great insentient";
yet here, one asks again in terms of the "great" and "small. This is likely because the previous [statement] addressed the Buddha-nature from a specific perspective.
Now, since this discussion is conducted within the context of the Middle Way (Madhyamaka), it applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;

however, regarding the Mahāyāna teachings, as for that which is called "insentient" (*niṣceṣṭa*), is it provisional (*neyārtha*) or ultimate (*nītārtha*)? It is not the provisional that is followed here; if it were ultimate, how could there even be the name "insentient"?

Next, the question "insentient things are non-existent" intends to ask: if insentient things are non-existent by nature because they are [merely] form (*rūpa*), then sentient beings (*sattva*) would likewise [be non-existent].

If you claim that form (*rūpa*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), yet consider that which is non-form to be insentient (*acetana*), then since non-form is precisely mind (*citta*), how could it lack intrinsic nature?
If both form and non-form are insentient, then since there is no sentient being outside these two dharmas, where could one seek intrinsic nature?
Third, regarding "insentient form and so forth," the "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers back to non-form; it may also be extended [to include other categories].
Regarding other objects such as these, whether they be material or immaterial, are they seen by the Buddha or are they seen by ordinary beings?
The Buddha sees them without duality; duality belongs to the views of ordinary beings. Now, does this accord with delusion or with awakening?

If it were a common perception, then since duality is non-dual and non-duality lacks intrinsic nature, how could there be a fixed distinction between sentient and insentient, or material and immaterial?

Fourth, regarding the question of insentient things being subject to decay: if it is argued that because they are subject to decay they are not the Buddha-nature, then the aggregates (*skandha*) of sentient beings are likewise subject to the nature of decay;
how could this be so? Fifth, regarding the question of insentient things being form (*rūpa*):

while all eight bases of the aggregates and elements possess form, the reason for specifically citing the "form" within the sphere of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-āyatana*) is that it refers to the form within the dharma-realm.
Form is but a small portion; to cite the few as a case for the many is merely to highlight the difficulty.
If such form is said to lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is the same as insentient matter; if it is said to possess intrinsic nature, then both [the internal and external] are form.
How can one exist and the other not? Therefore, none can escape this contradiction.
Question: Have you ever heard the expression "mind-only"? Answer: It is simply that the mind is diverse; it is not called "mind-only. Question:

Does the expression "mind-only" refer to the minds of both ordinary beings and sages? Answer: Whether referring to sages or ordinary beings, both positions entail faults. Question: Regarding the name "mind-only," does it mean that the mind creates, or is there no mind?
Or does it mean that the mind is created? Both positions entail faults. Question: Is it "mind-only," or is it also "form-only"?
If it is not merely form, is form not mind? [The opponent asks: Is it created solely by mind? Is it based solely on the support (āśraya) and the primary support (samanantarāśraya)?
Are the primary subject and object the same or different?
These are the third and fifth questions, which ask generally about "mind-only. The first question directly challenges it by means of its names; first, he says "son" (putra).

As for those who have heard [of this] before, it is because other schools also possess the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), which is said to negate external objects while consciousness expresses its own mind;
how much more so, then, regarding the present school’s discourse on "mind-only," wherein all phenomena tend toward and are none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
How, then, could one not have heard of this? If one has indeed heard it, then apart from the single mind, there is nothing else whatsoever.

How could the Dharma allow for difference? If there were difference, it would not be called "only" (*kevala*). As for your view that it is different from non-difference, you should know this for yourself.
Next, regarding the question of whether the mind of "mind-only" is mundane or sagely:

although it is said that both positions have faults, the intention is actually to correctly demonstrate the mundane mind. Thus, the preceding text asks: "Does the term 'mind-only' refer only to the true mind?"
If one penetrates the principle that all deluded thoughts are but mind-only, how could one further differentiate between the sentient and the insentient?
To do so would be the error of contradicting the common teaching of "mind-only. However, the very locus where the ordinary mind is mind-only is itself the holy mind;

if the holy were different from the ordinary, it would not be mind-only (one might also say that at the locus where the holy mind is mind-only, there is a total absence of both holy and ordinary). Thus, we know that in "mind-only" there is neither ordinary nor holy.
Whether obstructing ordinary beings or sages, all things are solely like this; what fault could there be in clarifying it? Regarding the three questions:

the phrase "the name 'mind-only' creates" (*weixin mingzao*) is a textual error where the character for "mind" (*xin*) has been altered [from "name"]. However, when one says that the name "mind-only" creates, it refers to what is called in the *Non-duality Gate* (*Fenbie ermen lun*):
"The form of mind is mind itself; mind is named 'transformation,' and transformation is named 'creation. This is merely a matter of abbreviation in the text. Since it is entirely mind-only...
Furthermore, regarding the act of creating, the locus of creation is, in its very substance, nothing other than mind; how could one say there is no "mind" that creates?
Since the entirety of creation is mind, how could there be a duality; how could one say there is an "insentient" that creates? Thus, both positions involve errors.
To claim that only the mind creates is also a textual abbreviation; it should rather have been stated as: "Only the mind creates. (Question 4: Only Mind)
Regarding the passage "As for form (rūpa), it is a layered expression; 'mind-only' (cittamātra) follows below," the term "mind-only" is used in contrast to "form.

However, since all phenomena of the six sense objects within the dharma-realm—including form and so forth—are mind-only, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* contains passages stating that there is not only "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) but also "form-only" (rūpamātra).
This is because, in the perfect teaching, it is logically necessary that all dharmas are thus; if one does not allow for "form-only," then form would not be mind.

If form were not mind, then form and mind would be external to one another; in that case, it would follow that form is not the Dharma-realm, and furthermore, the doctrine of "Mind-Only" would be untenable.
If [form] were merely form, then the attachment to it would naturally vanish. Regarding the five questions concerning that which is created by Mind-Only:

these creations do not go beyond the "support" (the environment) and the "supported" (the sentient beings). Now, we ask: are this support and the supported identical or different? We say they are different.

If all is merely created by the mind, then how can it be said that the "homogeneous" nature applies equally to both the environment (*bhājanaloka*) and its inhabitants (*sattvaloka*)? If the environment and its inhabitants were identical [to the Buddha-nature], how could there be any distinction between them?

Question: Does the measure of sentient beings differ because their nature differs? Answer: No. It is not so within [the nature itself]; if it were, it would not be called "nature. Question: Regarding sentient beings...

Are the four propositions regarding whether the deluded mind-nature is pervasive or non-pervasive identical to or different from those of the *puruṣa* (spiritual self)? Question: Do sentient beings possess nature?

Is it solely the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), or is it also the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), or also the nature of retribution (*vipākadhātu*)? Question: Are sentient beings originally deluded, while Buddhas are awakened?

Or, once the Buddha has already attained awakening, does he awaken to the delusions of sentient beings? Question: How many Buddha-natures are there within the single body of a sentient being? And how many [Buddha-bodies] are there within the single body of a Buddha?
How many births does this nature undergo?
The fourth and fifth questions collectively inquire regarding the limits of sentient beings as conceived by those [opponents].

If it is claimed that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, then just as there are various distinctions in the number and measure of sentient beings, so too should the Buddha-nature vary accordingly.

The opponent says: "If they were different, it would be impossible; if they were not different, then they would not be internal. Since you speak of them as being 'within the body,' how can they not be different?

Next, regarding the question of whether the deluded mind of sentient beings is pervasive: as stated in the preceding text, because the essence of the nature of the afflictions is pervasive, it is said that Buddha-nature is pervasive.
However, if one says it is not pervasive, then it cannot be pervasive; if it is pervasive, then it is identical to that which is external.

Regarding the four propositions concerning the Ātman—such as whether the self is large while matter is small, and so forth—as to whether they are identical or different: identity cannot be asserted, yet difference likewise cannot be maintained;

otherwise, it would not differ from the externalist views. Therefore, by what means can one reach certainty? It is said: because the substance of the mind alone is all-pervasive, it is naturally distinct from the calculations of externalists.
Third question: regarding whether the Buddha-nature of sentient beings has universal or limited application, this is discussed according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanlun).
The Buddha-nature of the three bodies has never for a moment been separated from the realm of sentient beings;
therefore, as the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-body) naturally penetrates the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, it is not obstructed by insentient things.

If one asks about the nature of insentient things, one should understand that through the *dharmakāya* it reaches the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*. Thus, while each term has its own specific application, that which is revealed is one and the same.

Question: Regarding the meaning of "sentient beings and Buddhas," "delusion and enlightenment": this indicates that although sentient beings and Buddhas differ, there is no distinction between delusion and enlightenment.

The place where sentient beings are deluded is precisely the place where all Buddhas are enlightened; the place where all Buddhas are enlightened is precisely the place where sentient beings are deluded.

Since the Buddha has manifested enlightenment such that his body and land are fused and pervasive, how could it be otherwise that the Buddha-nature exists within delusion as well? (The fifth question concerning the Buddha.)

Regarding the oneness and multiplicity of nature: although the natures of sentient beings and Buddhas inherently possess each other, when one speaks in terms of "aspects" (*ji*), this is intended as a question posed by way of negation;
the meaning must be reversed. If the natures of sentient beings and Buddhas are one, how could there be aspects?

Then one would also have to say: if Buddha-nature is one, how could there be the distinction between the sentient and the non-sentient? The superficial explanations of various schools all fail to [grasp this].
May you understand the intention of this author so that nothing remains hidden?
Question: Is the Buddha-land the beginning or the foundation of the Buddha-body? Are the beginning and the foundation the same, or are they different?

Question: Are the Buddha-land and the Buddha-body one or different? If they are one, there is neither subject nor object; if they are different, they are the same as ordinary beings. Question: Regarding the divisions of the Buddha-land and the arising of...
Furthermore, do the Buddhas each have their own respective abodes, or do they have no lands at all? Regarding what is encompassed by a Buddha-land, is it far or near?
Is that land identical to or distinct from its inhabitants, and are they common or separate? Are the essence of the Buddhas and the essence of their Buddha-lands the same or different?
And as for the place of this Sahā world, is it common or distinct?
The fifth section consists of five questions concerning the Buddha-land as a whole. The first question concerns the Buddha-land body (*buddhakṣetra-kāya*) as the beginning and the root.
It states that the "land-body" is one of the ten bodies of Vairocana according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

That it possesses the manifestation of the ten bodies is precisely the non-duality of the environment and the inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu* and *adhiṣṭhāna*). Now, this question asks about this land-body.
Is it that there is first existence, or is it that there is existence from the beginning? Are the beginning and the fundamental the same, or are they different?

To say they are different and that there is first existence is certainly not the case; yet to say they are the same and that there is existence from the beginning implies that the characteristic of non-duality already exists within the cause—how then can one say that insentient things lack Buddha-nature?
Next, the intention behind the question regarding whether the body and the land are identical or different is as follows:

By means of the integrated function of the Buddha’s fruition-body and its land, it is revealed that the sentient beings’ environment and its inhabitants (the *niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are likewise identical;

for if they are indeed identical, how could there be any insentient matter that differs from Buddha-nature? Third, regarding the question of whether the divisions of the Buddha-lands are common or distinct:

although three points are established as questions, they primarily reveal that sentient beings and Buddhas cohabit [the same realm]; for while the bodies and lands of sentient beings may differ, [they share the same reality].
The Buddha is such that the primary and secondary [realms] are without distinction; because they are without distinction, one verifies their constant fusion.
By means of the Buddha, the deluded attachment to birth is naturally resolved. Regarding the four questions concerning what lands are subsumed within the Buddha-lands and their relative distances:
since the Buddha necessarily subsumes all four lands, if one were to discuss their distances and sequence, it would likewise be evident. Now, this questioner asks only which land [is meant].

Regarding the commonality and distinction between [the Buddha-land] and birth: while the term "birth" applies generally to the three lands, the specific distinction lies in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
The meaning of "commonality and distinction" is intended to clarify what has been stated above (etc.). Fifth, concerning the substance of the Buddha’s Buddha-land:

whereas previously the question was posed in contrast to "birth," the present inquiry is made from the Buddha's own perspective. If we discuss it in a general sense, is the substance of the Buddha’s Buddha-land identical or different?
If one must speak of them as identical, then regarding the realm of Sahā, one must say they are distinct;

yet, since it has not been seen what the underlying principle revealed here is, one must further understand the so-called "simultaneous identity. If all things were identical in essence, then everything would be the four [realms];
however, in reality, they have never been identical. One must know that whether horizontal or vertical, they reside in but a single place; thus, in reality, they are distinct.
If one has never perceived them as distinct, then the dharma-realm would be eternally identical and eternally different; what would be identical and what would be different?
Who would be common and who would be separate? Ultimately speaking, when seeking the body and the land, they are utterly unobtainable;
how then could there be such things as the sentient and the insentient?
Question: When the Buddha attained enlightenment, did the land also attain it? Did it become vast or narrow? If you say it did not, there is a fault. Question:
Is the Buddha’s attainment of the nature of seeing the same as or different from the place where seeing arises? It cannot be asked if it is distinct from both. Question:
Are the Buddha’s attainment of the land and their respective attainments and non-attainments one or different? Question: Are the Buddha’s three bodies the same as those respective fruits?

Furthermore, regarding those various births, are they one or different? [The text] asks: when a Buddha manifests his body and land (*kāya-bhūmi*), what kind of eyes, wisdom, and vision does he employ to perceive the realms of self and others, and how are these [perceptions] at the beginning and at the end?
These six questions and five inquiries collectively concern the manifestation of the Buddha’s body and land. The first question concerns whether or not the Buddha-land is manifested.
Now, the discourse on the realization of the Way is ultimately difficult to express; yet, within that which is ineffable, I shall attempt to speak of it briefly.
One must realize the essence of Great Perfect Enlightenment within all phenomena and attain the great function of the Dharma-realm before one can be said to have perfected the Way.
Thus, once perfected, all is perfected; by following and relying upon this correct turning, mountains, rivers, and nations [are transformed].

There is no land that is not entirely perfected; this is what is called the body and land of Vairocana. It is not something that can be conjectured or measured by the conceptualizing mind. Therefore it is said:
"When one Buddha attains enlightenment, the entire Dharma-realm is none other than the environment and the body of this Buddha.

And again: "When the fruit of the three thousandfold world-system is realized, all are termed eternal and blissful. These are the inherent principles of reality, not merely the tenets of a single school.
I say this: the one who now speaks asks whether the earth is formed, or whether its formation has breadth or narrowness. This too is not a question that should be asked.
If he were to say it is not formed, then since it is already formed, how could there be breadth or narrowness?

If there is no breadth or narrowness, how can one distinguish between the sentient and the insentient? If one says it is not formed, there is a fault; for there would be a contradiction regarding both the body and the earth.
This is the error of Cheng. Next, he asked whether the Buddha’s realization of the nature and the place where one gives rise to views are the same or different.

He meant that if they are different, then the place is the same; if they are the same, then the seeing is distinct. Examining the difference through their sameness, it must be that one is real and the other is false.

Furthermore, if the Buddha sees the nature, then [the nature] is the same, while what is seen by ordinary beings is different. Or, if the seeing is different, then difference is itself sameness—just as with the ordinary person.
The perception [of them] is identical to that of the sentient beings of those respective lands; thus, these two meanings are not different but identical.
Since there can be nothing other than being either identical or different, it is said: "Apart from these two, a third is impossible. Question:

When one speaks of identity or difference based on whether a single Buddha-land is established for each respective birth of a Buddha, or whether such establishment occurs or does not occur, why is it said that difference is certainly impossible, yet identity is also not possible?
The meaning of the four questions cannot be divided; it is the same as above, but regarding the three bodies (*trikāya*) in relation to their respective fruits, those fruits are thereby established.

As for the statement that "their respective births and lives are not established," this is merely a difference in phrasing. The fifth question summarizes the aforementioned accomplishment of the body and land;
the eyes and wisdom are clearly the Buddha-eye and the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-knowing wisdom). "The objects of self and others" refers to the aforementioned birth of the Buddha.
Although the objective realm is thus, when viewed through the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of all modes, self and other are one and the beginning and end are non-dual;
how, then, could there be any perception of distinctions between bodies and lands?
Question: Regarding that which is produced by True Suchness (*tathatā*), do these things mutually encompass one another or not? How is it in either case? Question:
Does the essence of True Suchness pervade both the cultivated (*xiu*) and the innate (*xing*), as well as the body and the land, or are they unequal?

Question: When True Suchness follows conditions and transforms into insentient matter, is it permanently insentient? When will it ever become sentient again? Question: Once True Suchness has followed conditions and transformed, how does it relate to True Suchness itself?

Are they identical or different? Are they eternally concomitant? Is true suchness (tathatā) originally existent or originally non-existent? How does it coexist with afflictions (kleśa), and what is their relationship of identity or difference?
These five questions of the seventh [section] collectively inquire about true suchness. The first question concerns the inclusion of the marks produced by true suchness.

Regarding "not being mutually inclusive," these terms such as "mutual inclusion" apply to both aspects [the principle and the phenomena]. If one discusses them in terms of phenomena and principle, then True Suchness (tathatā) is the principle and that which is produced is the phenomenon.
This means that if there is inclusion, the phenomenon and the principle must be fused; if there is no inclusion, how could they possibly be separated?
If discussed in terms of phenomena alone, then the environments and inhabitants of the ten realms are none other than True Suchness following along with them.

Regarding whether that which is conditioned by conditions is subsumed or not subsumed [within the nature], this follows the same logic as the previous objection; how can these two positions both be established?
Next, concerning whether True Suchness (tathatā) is differentiated or undifferentiated:

since True Suchness has no separate self-substance, taking all phenomena as its substance, it encompasses both the cultivated and the innate, and pervades both body and land; indeed, there is nothing to which it does not apply. Thus, everything is True Suchness.
Since the cultivated nature-body and its lands are none other than True Suchness (tathatā), how could there be any inequality among them?
While inequality might still be conceivable, it is especially untenable here. Third, regarding the question of whether the insentient world transforms from the nature into existence or non-existence:
if you grant that the insentient originally transforms from the nature, how could that transformation be eternally non-existent? If it must indeed exist, then the future fruition will be established.
Furthermore, this reveals that by examining its beginning and end, one knows through the Buddha-nature that it is not eternally non-existent.
What then is meant by "making"? This is likely an error in the character used. Fourth question: Regarding True Suchness following conditions (*tathatā-anuvidhāna*), this encompasses two questions:

first, having followed conditions, does it return to being True Suchness, or does it follow conditions forever? Second, is there a True Suchness that is capable of following, and that which is followed...

If one follows the principle that "following conditions" is neither identical to nor different from [the nature], and realizes that "following conditions" is itself "unchanging," and "unchanging" is itself "following conditions," then these two questions will naturally be resolved.
The intent of the question thus reveals the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena. Regarding the fifth question concerning the existence or non-existence of *tathatā*:
although the question examines both aspects, its meaning ultimately returns to its inherent existence. If it is inherently existent, then...
If the nature of delusion is fundamentally identical [to the true nature], yet it is said that [the true nature] dwells together with delusion, how can one speak of their identity or difference?

This is because they do not understand the principle that the perfect [nature] is inherently endowed with all things; thus, for the time being, they find it difficult to resolve whether they are the same or different.

If one understands that the true and the false share a common source, then one may rely upon the single root of the correct and the provisional—how then could there be any distinction between emotional nature and essential nature?
Question: Regarding the similarities and differences between waves and water, their sequence and priority, and their gain and loss or truth and falsity—what are the analogies for these?

Regarding the presence or absence of flowers seen by diseased eyes, and the similarities and differences between the location of the flowers and the location of space—what are the analogies for these?

Regarding the mirror-image and its luminous substance, their origin and beginning, their similarities and differences, their sequence and priority, and their presence or absence—what are the analogies for these? And regarding the analogy of the Indra’s Net, does it illustrate only the fruit?

This is also like asking whether the cause has a fruit or whether the fruit is without a cause; it is like asking whether the body of the wish-fulfilling jewel possesses a land, or whether it exists only in the fruit, or how it pervades both cause and fruit.
The eighth and fifth questions are posed by means of various analogies. First, regarding the question of the similarities and differences between waves and water: this is—
The preceding passage states: "When it is in moisture, how could it be separated from the turbid and clear? As waves, they distinguish themselves as clear or turbid.
This refers to the identity and difference between the waves and the water. It further states: "One may only say that water is fundamentally without waves;

one must never say that there is no water within the waves. This refers to the gain and loss regarding what comes before and after. If one applies this to the current case of the identity of the true and the false:
Regarding difference, one should likewise say only that "the true is fundamentally without the false," but one must never say "within the false there is no true.

Thus, the fact that we currently perceive differences between the environment and its inhabitants, or between the sentient and the insentient, is the false; how could it be that there is no Buddha-nature which is truly identical?
Therefore, it is said: "How are the Dharma and the analogy? Let them answer for themselves, and their success or failure will be evident. Next:

Regarding the question of the existence and disappearance of flowers in the sky: the intent is to use "emptiness" as a metaphor for the awakened nature (*bodhata*) and "flowers" as a metaphor for the environment and its inhabitants.

Since emptiness is fundamentally devoid of flowers, which appear only due to an eye ailment, so too is the awakened nature devoid of environment and inhabitants, which appear only due to emotional views.

Thus, the locus of emptiness is itself the locus of the flowers; when the flowers vanish, emptiness remains. If the perception of environment and inhabitants were not false, then the awakened nature— [...would likewise remain]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.)
This emptiness is inherently hidden. If one says that insentient things lack Buddha-nature, it is largely like seeing the flower but not seeing the emptiness.
Is this to be considered understanding or delusion? Third, regarding the mirror-image:

although the single metaphor of the mirror-image is used in various texts—sometimes to illustrate the three dharmas, or sometimes to illustrate cultivation and nature (and so forth)—in this case, it is none of these.
Taking the image within the mirror directly as a metaphor for the primary and secondary [bodies], and the luminous substance of the mirror as a metaphor for *buddha-nature*:
since the image necessarily exists in dependence upon the luminosity, on one hand the mirror’s luminosity is the basis and the manifested image is the beginning;

yet because the luminosity is revealed through the image, the image comes first and the luminosity follows. If one discusses their identity and difference based on this, they are said to be different.
Thus, apart from luminosity there are no images; what is called "sameness" means that the mind possesses luminosity.
Although images appear and disappear, the mirror's luminosity remains constant. Precisely because it remains constant, when there are images, there is luminosity.

To speak in terms of the Dharma, both the primary and secondary [elements] likewise possess an inherent nature (*dhātu*). If the images were not luminous, then even sentient beings would be non-existent.
Reflect upon this by applying the analogy to the dharma; it can be understood through the nature [of the analogy]. Fourth, regarding the analogy of Indra’s net:

Indra’s net is used as a metaphor for the mutual integration of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), wherein taking up one part encompasses the whole, and each element is mutually non-obstructive.

If it were merely an analogy for the fruit, there would be no cause; yet if it also serves as an analogy for the cause, the cause must necessarily encompass the fruit. Therefore, how could the interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants pertain solely to the fruit?

Regarding the "upper body of earth," there are five questions. As for the "wish-fulfilling jewel body," this is fundamentally a metaphor for manifesting forms according to the various capacities of beings within the state of fruition (*phala*);
